descriptions.active_avg: Average of months with spending only — ideal for irregular expenses
descriptions.banded_avg: Average of recent months, bounded by a floor and ceiling you define
descriptions.declining_target: Gradually reduces the limit each month to help cut a recurring expense
descriptions.envelope_rollover: What you don't spend one month raises your limit the next
descriptions.historical_max: Historical maximum with a safety margin
descriptions.income_pct: Percentage of the period's average income
descriptions.median: Your typical month's value — immune to outlier months
descriptions.percentile_n: A limit that would cover most of your recent months
descriptions.seasonal_yoy: Combines the same month from last year with your recent average — for seasonal expenses
descriptions.simple_avg: Average spending over the last N months
descriptions.sinking_fund: Spreads a planned annual expense into equal monthly installments
descriptions.trimmed_mean: Average excluding the most extreme months in the period

examples.active_avg: Gifts: 400 in three of the last twelve months. A plain average would say 100; this one says 400 — what it actually costs when it happens.
examples.banded_avg: Electricity: follows the average, with a floor of 200 (the bill never comes in lower) and a ceiling of 500 (above that you want to be warned).
examples.declining_target: Takeout: starts from your average and asks for 5% less each month, down to the floor you set.
examples.envelope_rollover: Clothing: two months without buying anything raise the limit for the month you finally do.
examples.fixed_target: Subscriptions: you decided it never goes above 150 a month, whatever you spent before.
examples.historical_max: Health: if the worst month was 900, the limit lands at 990 with a 10% margin — a rough month no longer trips a false alarm.
examples.income_pct: Leisure at 10% of what comes in: in a leaner month, the limit drops on its own.
examples.median: Maintenance: eleven months near 200 and one at 3,000. The average would say 430; the median says 200.
examples.moving_avg: Rent raised two months ago: recent months weigh more and the limit follows, without waiting for the increase to soak into the average.
examples.percentile_n: Fuel at the 75th percentile: three out of four months fit the limit; the fourth is an exception you accept.
examples.seasonal_yoy: School supplies: instead of the quiet months that just passed, it looks at the same month a year earlier.
examples.simple_avg: Groceries: 1,800, 2,200 and 1,600 over the last three months become a limit of 1,867.
examples.sinking_fund: An annual 2,400 insurance bill due in 12 months: the monthly limit becomes 200 starting now.
examples.trimmed_mean: Food with one travel month (very high) and one month away on holiday (very low): both drop out of the calculation.

whenToUse.active_avg: For expenses that don't show up every month. A plain average divides by the empty months and produces a ceiling far too low for the month the expense actually lands.
whenToUse.banded_avg: When you accept following the average, but within bounds: never below the minimum the bill demands, never above what you're willing to spend.
whenToUse.declining_target: When the goal is to cut an expense step by step rather than track it. Each month asks for a little less than the last.
whenToUse.envelope_rollover: When what's left over should stay yours: the unspent amount becomes slack in the following months instead of evaporating at month's end.
whenToUse.fixed_target: When the amount is your decision, not a consequence of history: contracts, fixed transfers, negotiated caps.
whenToUse.historical_max: When overshooting is worse than having money left over. The limit covers even the worst month in the period, plus a margin — good for expenses you can't postpone.
whenToUse.income_pct: When the ceiling should depend on what comes in, not on what went out. Useful for variable income and for setting aside a fixed share.
whenToUse.median: When one or two off-pattern months distort the average. The median describes the typical month and ignores the exceptional one.
whenToUse.moving_avg: When your pattern changed recently and a plain average still carries months that no longer apply.
whenToUse.percentile_n: When you want to choose how much slack you get: a limit that would have covered most months, not every one.
whenToUse.seasonal_yoy: For expenses with a season, where the same month a year earlier predicts better than the recent months do.
whenToUse.simple_avg: For expenses that vary little from month to month, when you want a limit that tracks your real pace.
whenToUse.sinking_fund: When a large, expected expense arrives all at once and you'd rather set money aside monthly than absorb the hit.
whenToUse.trimmed_mean: When you want the average without the extremes on either side: neither the nearly idle month nor the exceptional one.
